Anthropic record IPO and Nvidia results beat can't stop the slide
Hi there!

It was a busy week all round. The ASX 200 touched five-month lows on Friday after a week-long miners and commodities sell-off. Jensen Huang asked for his job back as CEO of Nvidia and had the door firmly closed on him.

Nvidia posted third-quarter results that beat analyst expectations pretty much across the board and raised its outlook for next year, but its shares fell. Anthropic became the seventh most valuable US company after its record-breaking US$81.3 billion IPO — US$107 billion including a concurrent private placement — and major US benchmarks still fell over 2%, extending losses for the week. And to top it off, global stocks are on track for their longest losing streak since September 2023, based on the MSCI All Country World Index.
It was a week where the good news, however bright, was not able to overturn the dominant risk-off trend. Talking about trends… Carl’s ChartWatchpretty much nailed all of them!
On a side note – it’ll be a clipped version of the weekender for the next two weeks while Kerry is away.
Let’s dive in!

Best of Livewire
Here are some of my favourite reads from our friends at Livewire.

Takeovers galore: who’s next?: Keith Ford breaks down Macquarie’s updated takeover screen that picks six ASX stocks trading well below their highs, including ARB, Domino’s, EBOS and IPH. Nearly half the stocks on its first list in 2020 have since been involved in some form of M&A.

How safe is your job?: Carl Capolingua unpacks October’s 43,500 job losses, which pushed unemployment to 4.9% with part-timers hit hardest. Morgan Stanley expects the RBA to hold at 4.85% through the first half of 2027 before cutting twice.

The AI bubble has already burst: Plato’s David Allen points out Goldman’s AI beneficiaries basket has fallen almost 30% since 30 June while AI at-risk names rose almost 50%. He argues Nvidia on 16 times forward earnings and Alphabet on 15 times are hardly bubble valuations.

The infrastructure boom never ended: First Sentier’s Peter Meany says utilities are now growing 8-10% a year, up from a historical 5-6%, as hyperscalers sign long-term power contracts. He prefers US utilities, which he finds easier to navigate on regulation and politics.

Where to park your cash: 10 ASX ETFs: Patrick Poke compares savings accounts paying up to 6.5% with ten cash and floating-rate ETFs. AAA yields 4.92% after fees, so the case for listed options rests on balance caps, eligibility and convenience rather than return.
